column2: Lost revenue that can be claimed
Economic damage — caused by a third party
Deemed under the deemed energy clause
The real shortfall: the deemed energy portion has been deducted.
Energy lost × price. The deemed portion is not yet deducted — see "Lost revenue" for the real shortfall.
The value of the energy lost attributed to warranty and to O&M contract obligations. THIS IS NOT YET THE RECOVERABLE AMOUNT.
Genuinely lost with nobody to claim from. Kept apart so it is not confused with the part the owner bears through poor management.
Derived from the START time. An outage spanning two periods still counts wholly in the period it started in — see the "spans two periods" flag.
The part caused by the grid that the power purchase agreement still pays for. The share comes from the period's own contract, not a default of 100%.
The part of the availability loss whose cause the outage log cannot identify. This is where money leaks away with nobody claiming it.
The value of the shortfall BELOW THE AVAILABILITY COMMITMENT. Above the commitment the contractor owes nothing, even though the energy is still lost.
The number of outages declaring lost MWh on a time category of "no energy there to lose" — below cut-in wind speed, nothing is lost.
The REAL shortfall = the value of the energy lost − the deemed portion. An outage caused by grid curtailment has a large energy value but a shortfall of zero.
Cross-check against the period's "Curtailed" field. Under IEC 61400-26 curtailment is NOT downtime — the machine remains available — so it does not enter the availability denominator.

The outage ends in a different period from the one it started in. For now it counts wholly in the starting period — it is not yet apportioned. This flag marks where the figure is not quite exact, rather than hiding it.

Only CHILD outages are summed — the root outage of an incident spanning several machines is excluded to avoid double counting. And only the categories valued as a genuine loss are summed: grid curtailment sits in a column of its own.

A WEIGHTED AVERAGE price by that period's own energy. Where a project sells to several offtakers at different prices, the energy lost has to be valued at the real weighting rather than at one contract's price.
Decides whether energy lost under this category enters lost revenue. The system pre-fills it, but it is EDITABLE: on a project with no deemed energy clause, grid curtailment is a genuine loss.

Derived from the period's own availability percentage: the energy that would have been achieved at 100% availability. This is the denominator for cross-checking the outage log — DIFFERENT from "Availability shortfall", which is only the part below the commitment, that is, the part recoverable from the contractor.

Explained MWh ÷ loss from unavailability. Below 100% means THERE IS ENERGY LOST THAT NOBODY KNOWS THE REASON FOR — so look at this figure before believing any availability report. Above 100% means the log records more than was really lost: overlapping outages, or MWh estimated too generously.

Takes the LOWER of the damage caused by a third party and the contractual liability cap. It is still an ESTIMATE: the O&M contract's availability regime has its own formula, an annual liability cap, and usually excludes grid or force majeure hours from the availability denominator. This figure is for negotiating with, not for the books.

Cross-check on "Lost to unavailability", claim on "Availability shortfall". The two figures diverge widely: a 98% availability commitment means 2% of downtime is allowed to happen — energy lost that nobody has to pay for.
Coverage below 100% means there is energy lost that nobody knows the reason for. Look at this figure before believing any availability report, including your own.
Recoverable loss is still a figure for negotiating. An O&M contract's regime has its own availability penalty formula, an annual liability cap, and usually excludes grid or force majeure hours from the availability denominator.
